client: I've been struggling a lot since my mom passed away six months ago. It feels like everyone around me has just... moved on, like it was nothing, but I'm still completely stuck in this grief and I don't know how to function some days. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that what you're carrying sounds genuinely heavy and isolating, like you're grieving in a world that has moved on without you. Grief doesn't follow anyone else's timeline, and feeling stuck six months in isn't a sign that something is wrong with you — it's a sign of how much your mom meant to you. I'm wondering, when you say you don't know how to function some days, what does that tend to look like for you?

client: Some days I'll just sit in the same spot for hours and not be able to make myself do basic things, like eat or answer messages from people. I'll start to do something and then I'll think about how I used to call her when something happened, good or bad, and then it just hits me all over again that I can't do that anymore. It's like there's this wall between me and everything else, and I don't know how to get through it.
therapist: What you're describing — that moment where you reach for her and then remember — sounds like one of the most painful parts of grief, almost like losing her again in small ways throughout each day. That wall you're feeling isn't weakness; it's actually your mind and body trying to protect you from something almost too big to process all at once. I'm curious — when you think about those moments where you'd normally call her, what kinds of things would you have wanted to share with her?

client: Honestly, it could be anything — like last week I got a small promotion at work and my first instinct was to pick up the phone and call her, and then I just felt this wave of guilt, like how can I even feel good about something when she's not here to share it. Or sometimes it's just stupid little things, like I saw a recipe I know she would have loved and I just completely fell apart in the grocery store. It's embarrassing how unpredictable it is.
therapist: First, please know there is nothing embarrassing about falling apart in a grocery store — those small, unexpected moments can carry so much weight, and they actually speak to the depth and tenderness of your relationship with her. I also want to gently notice something: you got a promotion, which is genuinely wonderful, and your very first instinct was to share it with her — that impulse came from love, not something to feel guilty about. I'm wondering, when that guilt shows up around feeling good about something, what does the voice in your head tend to tell you?

client: The voice basically tells me that feeling happy is a betrayal, like I don't have the right to move forward when she can't. It says things like "she'll never get to see any of this" and somehow that makes any good thing feel hollow or even cruel. I know logically that probably doesn't make sense, but in the moment it feels completely true and I can't just talk myself out of it.
therapist: That voice is telling you a really painful story — that joy and grief can't coexist, that moving forward means leaving her behind — and even though you can see logically it might not be true, in those moments it feels absolutely real and convincing. In CBT we'd call this a thought worth gently examining, because there's actually another way to look at it: what if feeling happy about your promotion *is* her legacy, a life she helped build and wanted for you? I'm curious — if your mom were here and could tell you how she'd want you to feel about that promotion, what do you think she would actually say?

client: I know she would have been so proud and she would have told me to celebrate, that's just who she was. But when I try to use that to make myself feel better, it almost makes it worse in a way, because then I just miss her even more intensely and it doesn't actually quiet the guilt. I guess I'm not sure how thinking about what she would have wanted is supposed to help when the whole problem is that she's not here to actually say it.
therapist: You're touching on something really honest and important here — that accessing her voice brings both comfort and a fresh wave of missing her, and that's not a failure of the technique, it's just the complicated truth of grief. You're right that it can't fully quiet the guilt yet, and I don't want to offer you something that feels like a shortcut past pain that deserves to be felt. I'm wondering though — when you notice that guilt telling you that you don't have the right to feel good, do you think that voice is actually something *she* would recognize as true, or is it something grief itself invented?

client: That's actually a hard question to sit with, because honestly, no, she would never have recognized that voice as true — she would have thought it was ridiculous that I was punishing myself. But even knowing that, the guilt doesn't just go away, it's like it has its own logic that exists separate from anything she actually believed or valued. I guess I'm starting to wonder if this guilt is more about me than about her, but I don't know what to do with that realization.
therapist: That realization — that the guilt belongs to you rather than to her — is actually a really significant and courageous insight, and it's worth sitting with rather than rushing past. It sounds like part of you is starting to separate your grief from a story you've been telling yourself, and that's often where things can begin to shift, even if the guilt doesn't disappear overnight. I'm curious — when you say the guilt is more about you, do you have any sense yet of what it might be protecting you from, or what it would feel like to let yourself off the hook even just a little?

client: I think maybe the guilt is protecting me from having to fully accept that she's gone, like as long as I'm suffering I'm still somehow connected to her, still honoring her. If I let myself feel good and move forward, it might mean really accepting that she's not coming back, and that feels terrifying in a way that's hard to even put into words. Letting myself off the hook sounds simple when you say it like that, but it honestly feels like it would cost me something I'm not ready to lose.
therapist: What you just named is profound and takes real courage to see — that the grief and guilt have become a way of staying close to her, and that healing feels like it might require a loss on top of a loss. That makes complete sense, and it's not something to just push through or logic your way past. I want to gently offer this though: what if staying connected to her didn't have to cost you your own life moving forward — what do you think *she* would say about being the reason you can't let yourself feel joy?

client: She would have been horrified, honestly — she would have said something like "don't you dare waste your life being sad for me." But knowing that and feeling it are such different things, and I guess I'm scared that if I find other ways to feel connected to her, they won't be real enough, like they'll just be things I'm doing to cope rather than actually keeping her present. I don't know how to stay close to someone who isn't here anymore without the grief being the thing that ties us together.
therapist: What you just said — "I don't know how to stay close to someone who isn't here anymore without the grief being the thing that ties us together" — might be the most important question you've brought here today, and it's one worth really honoring rather than rushing to answer. The fear that other connections to her would feel artificial makes so much sense, but I'd gently push back on one thing: the fact that you instinctively reached for the phone to tell her about your promotion, that you fell apart over a recipe she would have loved — those aren't grief, those are *her*, still alive in how you move through the world. I'm wondering, when you imagine what it might look like to carry her with you in those small moments — not as loss, but as her actual presence in who you've become — does any part of that feel possible, even slightly?

client: When you put it that way, yeah, a small part of me can see that — like those moments where I reach for the phone or fall apart over a recipe, maybe those aren't just painful reminders of what I lost but actually proof that she's still shaping how I experience things. But I'm worried that if I start thinking about it that way, I'll somehow convince myself I'm okay before I actually am, like I'll be performing healing instead of actually doing it. I guess I don't fully trust myself to know the difference right now.
therapist: That worry about "performing healing" rather than actually experiencing it shows a really deep self-awareness, and honestly, the fact that you're asking that question is itself a sign you're doing the real thing — people who are just going through the motions rarely worry this much about authenticity. Healing isn't a feeling you suddenly arrive at; it's more like a gradual shift where both the grief and the joy get to coexist, and you don't have to choose between honoring her and living your life. I'm curious — what do you think *actually* being okay would look like for you, not performing it, but genuinely feeling it?

client: I think actually being okay would mean being able to think about her and feel warmth instead of just pain, like remembering her laugh without it immediately turning into this crushing sadness. Maybe it would also mean being able to enjoy that promotion or other good things without the guilt hijacking everything, just letting myself have it. But even imagining that feels distant right now, almost like I'm describing a version of myself I can't quite picture yet.
therapist: What you just described — warmth instead of just pain, joy without guilt hijacking it — that's not a fantasy, that's actually a really clear and meaningful vision of where you want to get to, and having that picture matters even when it feels far away. The fact that you can imagine it at all, even as something distant, tells me that part of you already believes it's possible. I want to ask — looking back at everything you've shared today, even just in this conversation, do you notice anything that feels even slightly different from where you started?
